If a warning is issued for your location, act on it immediately — the median lead time is often well under an hour, and in steep terrain it can be minutes.

guides.title: Riverine Flooding and Floodplain Dynamics
guides.summary: How rivers generate floods, how floodplains are built and behave, how flood frequency is estimated and forecast, what defences do and fail to do, and how to act before, during and after a river flood.

sections.heading: What Riverine Flooding Is and Why It Is Its Own Hazard
sections.body: A riverine flood, also called a fluvial flood, occurs when the discharge of a river exceeds what its channel can carry, and water spills onto the adjacent land. That land is the floodplain, and it exists because the river built it out of its own sediment during previous floods. The essential point, which is easy to lose behind the language of disaster, is that a floodplain flooding is not a malfunction. It is the river operating normally. The flood is the mechanism by which the floodplain was constructed and by which it is maintained, and a river that never overtopped its banks would not have a floodplain at all. The hazard exists because people build on the flattest, most fertile, best-watered and most accessible land in the landscape, which happens to be the part the river uses periodically. Riverine flooding is worth distinguishing from the other kinds of flood, because the mechanism, the warning time and the correct response all differ. Pluvial or surface-water flooding happens when rain falls faster than the ground or the drains can absorb it, and can occur on a hilltop far from any river. Groundwater flooding occurs when the water table rises above ground level, usually slowly, and is characteristic of chalk and limestone catchments after a wet winter. Coastal flooding is driven by storm surge, tide and waves. Flash flooding is defined in most operational systems as flooding that begins within about six hours of the causative rainfall, and it can be riverine, in a small steep catchment, or pluvial, in a city. Dam-break and glacial lake outburst floods are riverine in their routing but catastrophic in their onset. Many real events are combinations: a tropical cyclone can produce surge, torrential pluvial flooding and a riverine flood peak arriving days later. The global significance is hard to overstate. Floods affect more people annually than any other natural hazard, with hundreds of millions exposed in a typical year, and something like 1.5 to 2 billion people live on land that has some meaningful annual chance of river flooding. The deadliest single natural disasters in recorded history are Chinese river floods, notably the 1931 Yangtze and Huai floods, whose death toll is variously estimated between several hundred thousand and several million and cannot now be determined. Economic losses have risen steadily in real terms almost everywhere, mostly because there is more of value on floodplains than there used to be, not because rivers have changed proportionately. One framing is worth adopting from the outset, because it organises everything else. Risk is not the same as hazard. The hazard is the flood: how deep, how fast, how often. The risk is what that flood does, which also depends on exposure, meaning what and who is in the way, and on vulnerability, meaning how badly they are hurt by a given depth of water. Almost all the growth in global flood losses over the past century is attributable to the second and third terms rather than the first, and almost all the opportunity to reduce losses lies there too.

sections.heading: The Catchment: How Rain Becomes Runoff
sections.body: Everything that happens in a river begins upstream in its catchment, also called its drainage basin or watershed, the entire area of land from which water drains to a given point. Rain falling on that area meets several possible fates, and which one dominates determines whether a storm produces a flood. Some rain is intercepted by vegetation and evaporates without ever reaching the ground; a dense forest canopy can intercept 10 to 30 per cent of a modest rainfall event, though a fraction of that in a heavy one. Some infiltrates the soil, where it may be held, taken up by plants, or move slowly downslope as throughflow, eventually reaching the river as the sustained baseflow that keeps it running between storms. The rest becomes overland flow, and overland flow is what makes floods. There are two distinct ways it forms, and the distinction matters. Infiltration-excess overland flow, described by Robert Horton in the 1930s, occurs when rainfall intensity exceeds the soil's infiltration capacity: the ground could hold more water but cannot accept it fast enough. This dominates on bare, crusted, compacted, frozen or paved surfaces and in intense convective storms, and it is the normal mechanism in arid and urban catchments. Saturation-excess overland flow, described by Thomas Dunne in the 1970s, occurs when the soil simply fills up, so that any further rain runs off regardless of intensity. This dominates in humid, vegetated catchments and appears first in valley bottoms and hollows where the water table is near the surface. The saturated area expands and contracts through a storm and between seasons, an idea known as the variable source area concept, which explains why the same rainfall can produce almost no runoff in September and a serious flood in February. That last point, antecedent conditions, is the single most under-appreciated control on flooding. A catchment already saturated by a wet month will convert a far higher fraction of the next storm into runoff than a dry one. Engineering practice captures this crudely through the curve number method developed by the United States Soil Conservation Service, which assigns each combination of soil group, land cover and antecedent wetness a number from about 30 to 98 and computes runoff depth from it. The physical shape of the basin matters too: steep slopes, high drainage density, thin soils, impermeable bedrock and a compact, circular basin outline all concentrate water quickly, while a long, narrow, gently sloping basin with deep permeable soils spreads the same water over days. A worked illustration makes the sensitivity concrete. Consider 100 millimetres of rain on a catchment of 50 square kilometres. If 20 per cent becomes runoff, that is 20 millimetres over 50 million square metres, or one million cubic metres of water. Delivered evenly over 24 hours it averages about 11.6 cubic metres per second, a substantial but manageable rise. If the catchment is already saturated and 60 per cent runs off, and steep terrain delivers it over six hours instead, the average becomes about 139 cubic metres per second and the instantaneous peak considerably more. Identical rainfall; a twelve-fold difference in flow.

sections.heading: The Flood Hydrograph: Lag, Peak and Recession
sections.body: A hydrograph is a plot of river discharge against time, and reading one is the core skill of practical hydrology. For a single storm it has a characteristic shape. Discharge begins at baseflow, the slow groundwater-fed contribution. When storm runoff begins to arrive, the curve turns upward into the rising limb, usually the steepest part. It reaches a maximum, the peak discharge, then declines along a recession limb that is always gentler than the rise, because the water still draining out of soils and shallow groundwater arrives progressively later. Eventually it returns to a baseflow that is often higher than before, since the storm recharged the groundwater. The interval between the centre of mass of the rainfall and the moment of peak discharge is the lag time, and it is the number that determines how much warning is possible. A small steep urban catchment of a few square kilometres may have a lag of thirty minutes; a rural catchment of a few hundred square kilometres, perhaps six to twelve hours; a great river such as the Mississippi or the Ganges, days to weeks. A hydrograph with a short lag and a sharp high peak is described as flashy, and flashiness is the product of steepness, impermeability, low storage and efficient drainage. Two further effects shape real hydrographs. The first is routing: as a flood wave travels downstream it spreads out in time and its peak attenuates, because the channel and floodplain temporarily store water on the rising limb and release it on the falling limb. A long, wide, well-connected floodplain is an extremely effective natural attenuator, and removing that storage by embanking a river is one of the principal ways engineering makes downstream floods worse. The second is the superposition of tributaries. The most dangerous situation in a large basin is not the largest rainfall but the coincidence of peaks: when two major tributaries deliver their maxima to a confluence at the same time, the combined peak can far exceed anything either could produce alone. Whether that coincidence happens depends on the shape of the storm, the direction it moved and the geometry of the network, which is why a storm tracking down a valley in the same direction as the flow is more dangerous than the same storm tracking up it. Leroy Sherman's unit hydrograph, introduced in 1932, formalised all this by defining the response of a catchment to one unit of effective rainfall in one unit of time, and then treating any storm as a linear superposition of such units. It is an approximation, since catchments are not linear, but it remains the conceptual backbone of practical flood estimation.

sections.heading: Channel Hydraulics: Discharge, Stage and the Rating Curve
sections.body: Discharge, denoted Q, is the volume of water passing a cross-section per unit time, expressed in cubic metres per second. It is the product of the cross-sectional area of flow and the mean velocity: Q equals A times v. A modest lowland river might carry 20 cubic metres per second in normal conditions and 400 in flood; the Amazon averages around 209,000. Velocity in an open channel is usually estimated with the Manning equation, published in 1889, which states that mean velocity equals one over n, multiplied by the hydraulic radius raised to the power two thirds, multiplied by the square root of the energy slope. The hydraulic radius is the cross-sectional area divided by the wetted perimeter, and it is a measure of hydraulic efficiency: a deep compact channel has a large hydraulic radius and moves water fast, while a wide shallow one has a small radius and moves it slowly. Manning's n is a roughness coefficient, and typical values are instructive. Smooth concrete is about 0.012, a clean straight earth channel about 0.025, a natural winding channel with stones and weeds about 0.035 to 0.05, and a floodplain covered in dense brush or standing timber 0.10 or more. Because velocity is inversely proportional to n, a floodplain three times rougher than the channel conveys water at roughly a third of the speed at the same depth and slope, which is exactly why floodplains store water rather than transmitting it. What is actually measured at a gauging station is not discharge but stage, the water surface elevation relative to a fixed datum, because stage is cheap and easy to record continuously with a float in a stilling well, a pressure transducer or a downward-looking radar. Discharge is then inferred using a rating curve, an empirically fitted relationship between stage and discharge built from repeated gaugings in which velocity is actually measured across the section with a current meter or acoustic profiler. The rating curve is the weak link in flood hydrology, and understanding why matters. Gaugings are made at the flows that occur most often, which are the low and moderate ones; the largest floods are rare, dangerous and sometimes physically impossible to measure. Extreme discharges are therefore usually obtained by extrapolating the curve beyond any measured point, and errors of 20 per cent or more at the top of the range are common. Worse, the relationship can shift. Bed scour or deposition during a flood changes the channel geometry, so the same stage no longer corresponds to the same discharge. When water leaves the channel and spreads across the floodplain the effective section changes character entirely. And an unsteady flood wave produces hysteresis, in which discharge on the rising limb exceeds discharge on the falling limb at identical stage, because the water surface slope is steeper while the wave is arriving. A published peak discharge for a historic flood should always be read as an estimate with real uncertainty, not a measurement.

sections.heading: Bankfull Discharge and the Making of a Floodplain
sections.body: Rivers are not sized for their largest floods. A channel adjusts its width, depth and slope over decades and centuries to the flows that do most of the geomorphic work, and the resulting capacity is called the bankfull discharge: the flow that exactly fills the channel to the top of its banks without spilling over. In the classic work of Luna Leopold, Gordon Wolman and John Miller in the early 1960s, bankfull discharge in humid temperate rivers was found to recur roughly once every one to two years, a figure often quoted as 1.5 years. The value varies by climate, but the principle holds: a river is built to contain a flow it experiences most years and to overflow at anything much larger. The underlying reasoning was set out by Wolman and Miller in 1960 in terms of effective discharge. The total geomorphic work a river does at any given flow is the product of how much sediment it moves at that flow and how often that flow occurs. Very large floods move enormous quantities of sediment but happen rarely; very small flows happen constantly but move almost nothing. The product peaks somewhere in the middle, at moderately frequent flows near bankfull, and that is where most of the channel and floodplain get built. Floodplain construction happens by two complementary processes. Lateral accretion occurs as a meandering channel erodes its outer bank, where velocity and shear stress are highest, and deposits on the inner bank as a point bar, where flow is slower. Over time the channel migrates sideways, paving the valley floor with successive point-bar deposits of coarse sand and gravel that make up the bulk of many floodplains by volume. Vertical accretion occurs during overbank floods: water leaving the channel decelerates abruptly, loses its capacity to carry sediment, and drops it, coarser material immediately beside the channel and progressively finer silt and clay farther out. A floodplain is therefore a layered structure of channel sands overlain by overbank muds, and its stratigraphy can be read as a record of the river's history. This has a direct practical consequence. The extent of the floodplain visible in the landscape, the flat valley floor bounded by a distinct break in slope, is itself a flood hazard map drawn by the river over thousands of years. It is more reliable in some respects than any model, because it records what the river has actually done rather than what an equation predicts it might. Channel geometry follows regular empirical patterns that are useful in the field. Meander wavelength is typically ten to fourteen times the channel width, and the radius of curvature of a bend about two to three times the width, so the scale of a river's meander belt can be estimated from its width alone. Sinuosity, the ratio of channel length to straight valley length, exceeds about 1.5 in a fully meandering river. These relationships mean that where a river appears unnaturally straight and its floodplain unnaturally narrow, it has almost always been engineered, and its flood behaviour will not resemble that of its unmodified reaches.

sections.heading: Floodplain Landforms and How to Read Them
sections.body: A floodplain that looks flat from a car window resolves into distinct landforms when examined closely, and each carries information about flood behaviour. Natural levees are low ridges of coarser sediment flanking the channel, built because overbank flow decelerates most sharply as it crosses the bank line and deposits its heaviest load immediately. They are typically a few tens of centimetres to a few metres high and slope gently away from the river. Their existence produces the counter-intuitive result that the highest ground on many floodplains is right next to the river, which is why villages, roads and railways so often occupy the levee crest, and why once a river does overtop, the water flows away from the channel and cannot easily return. Behind the levees lie backswamps: low, poorly drained areas of fine silt and clay that hold water long after the river has fallen. Where a levee is breached during a flood, a fan of sand called a crevasse splay is deposited into the backswamp behind it, and repeated breaching at one point can eventually lead the river to abandon its channel entirely and take a shorter, steeper course, a process called avulsion. Avulsion lies behind the most catastrophic river changes in history, including the repeated relocations of China's Yellow River, which has shifted its mouth by hundreds of kilometres several times within the historical record. Meandering channels leave a rich record. Cutoffs occur when the neck of a meander loop is breached and the loop is abandoned, leaving a crescent-shaped oxbow lake that gradually fills with fine sediment and organic matter. Scroll bars, arcuate ridges and swales preserved across the floodplain surface, trace the successive positions of point bars and are strikingly visible in aerial imagery. Yazoo tributaries run parallel to the main river for long distances, trapped behind its natural levee until a low point is found; the name comes from the Yazoo, which parallels the Mississippi for about 280 kilometres. Terraces are the most important feature for anyone assessing risk. A terrace is an abandoned floodplain, left stranded above the modern one after the river incised, and it is recognisable as a flat bench with a distinct step down to the active floodplain. Terraces flood only in extraordinary events or not at all, and the boundary between terrace and floodplain, often just a metre or two of elevation, is frequently the sharpest real line between safe and unsafe ground in a river valley. Reading these features in the field or on aerial imagery is a practical skill with real value. Oxbows, scroll bars, subtle levee ridges and abrupt breaks in slope are all visible in good shaded-relief imagery derived from airborne lidar, and they map the ground the river has occupied within the last few thousand years far more directly than a hydraulic model does. Where a modelled flood extent and the geomorphic evidence disagree, the geomorphology deserves at least equal weight, because it is a record of events rather than a prediction of them, and it captures processes such as avulsion and channel migration that conventional flood models do not represent at all.

sections.heading: Flood Frequency and What a Hundred-Year Flood Really Is
sections.body: Flood frequency analysis assigns probabilities to flood magnitudes. The standard procedure takes the largest instantaneous discharge in each year of record, the annual maximum series, ranks those values, fits a statistical distribution to them, and reads off the magnitude corresponding to any chosen probability. Common choices of distribution include the generalised extreme value, the Gumbel, the generalised logistic used in British practice, and the log-Pearson type III mandated in United States federal practice by Bulletin 17B and its successor 17C. The result is expressed either as an annual exceedance probability or as a return period, which is simply its reciprocal. A flood with a 1 per cent annual exceedance probability has a return period of 100 years and is universally called the hundred-year flood. That name causes more misunderstanding than any other term in hydrology. It does not mean the flood happens once a century, that having had one you are safe for ninety-nine years, or that it recurs on a schedule. It means that in any given year there is a 1 in 100 chance of a flood of that size or larger, independently of what happened last year. Two hundred-year floods in successive years are unremarkable; the probability of that specific pair is one in ten thousand, but there are a great many rivers and a great many years. The arithmetic that people actually need is the probability of experiencing at least one such flood over a period of years, which is one minus the probability of avoiding it every year: 1 minus (1 minus p) raised to the power n. For the hundred-year flood over a thirty-year mortgage, that is 1 minus 0.99 to the thirtieth power, which equals 0.26. There is a 26 per cent chance, better than one in four, that a house in the hundred-year floodplain floods during a single thirty-year mortgage. Over a seventy-year lifetime the figure is about 50 per cent. Anyone who thinks of the hundred-year floodplain as safe has misread the number by a wide margin. Three caveats limit all of this. First, uncertainty: estimating a 1 per cent flood from a thirty-year record is a long extrapolation, and the 95 per cent confidence interval on such an estimate is often plus or minus 30 to 50 per cent of the central value, which is rarely shown on a flood map. Second, non-stationarity: the entire method assumes the statistical properties of the flood series are constant through time, an assumption undermined by land use change, dam construction and a warming climate, and declared dead in an influential 2008 paper by Milly and colleagues. Third, a mapped flood extent depends not only on the discharge estimate but on the hydraulic model and terrain data used to convert discharge into a water surface, each with its own errors.

sections.heading: Kinds of Riverine Flood and Their Distinct Signatures
sections.body: Riverine floods are generated by several physically distinct mechanisms, and each has a characteristic season, duration, predictability and failure mode. Rainfall floods from large-scale frontal or monsoonal systems are the classic long-duration river flood: days of moderate rain over a large basin, a slow rise, a broad peak lasting days or weeks and a slow fall. These are the most forecastable floods, with lead times of days on major rivers. The Ganges, Brahmaputra, Mekong and Indus flood this way every summer, and the flooding is expected and to a large degree relied upon by agriculture. Convective rainfall floods are the opposite: extreme intensity over a small area for a few hours. In a small steep catchment the result is a flash flood with a lag of an hour or less, a violent peak and little or no warning. Tropical cyclones can deliver either or both; Hurricane Harvey in 2017 dropped over 1,500 millimetres on parts of southeast Texas, producing simultaneous urban pluvial flooding and a prolonged riverine flood. Snowmelt floods occur in spring in continental and mountain basins, and their magnitude depends on the water content of the snowpack, the speed of warming and whether the ground beneath is still frozen. Frozen ground has essentially zero infiltration capacity, so nearly all melt becomes runoff. Rain-on-snow events are particularly dangerous because rain adds water while also delivering latent heat that accelerates melting. Ice-jam floods occur during freeze-up or, more commonly, during spring breakup, when broken ice floes accumulate at a constriction, bend or bridge and form a dam. Stage upstream can rise several metres in under an hour, at discharges far below any conventional flood threshold, and when the jam releases a surge travels downstream. Ice-jam floods are poorly captured by standard frequency analysis because the controlling variable is not discharge. Outburst floods are the extreme tail. A landslide or moraine dam impounding a lake can fail suddenly; glacial lake outburst floods, known in Iceland as jokulhlaups, can release volumes over hours that dwarf any meteorological flood, and they are an increasing hazard in the Himalaya and Andes as glaciers retreat and leave unstable moraine-dammed lakes. Engineered dam failures belong here too: the collapse of the South Fork dam above Johnstown, Pennsylvania in 1889 killed over 2,200 people in minutes, and the failure of the Banqiao and Shimantan dams in Henan, China in August 1975 during an extraordinary typhoon rainfall caused a cascade of failures and a death toll estimated in the tens to over a hundred thousand. One further category deserves mention because it is entirely artificial: operational failure. Floods have been caused or made substantially worse by mistimed reservoir releases, by gates that could not be opened because power was lost, by pumping stations that flooded and stopped, and by debris blocking culverts and bridge openings so that water backed up behind an accidental dam and then released when it cleared. These failures are individually mundane and collectively responsible for a significant share of damage in developed catchments.

sections.heading: Sediment: Erosion, Transport and Deposition in Flood
sections.body: A flood is not just water. It is a sediment transport event, and most of the geomorphic change a river experiences in a decade happens during a handful of days of high flow. Rivers carry sediment three ways. Dissolved load is material in solution, unaffected by velocity. Suspended load is silt and clay held aloft by turbulence, what makes floodwater brown, and usually the majority of total load by mass in lowland rivers. Bed load is the coarser sand, gravel and cobbles that roll, slide and bounce along the bed, and although it is usually a minority of the mass it does most of the work of shaping the channel. Whether a given particle moves depends on the shear stress the flow exerts on the bed, which rises with depth and slope. The threshold at which motion begins is described by the Shields criterion, and the relationship between velocity and the size of grain that can be eroded, transported or deposited was summarised in the Hjulstrom curve of 1935. That curve contains one genuinely surprising result: fine clays require higher velocities to erode than sands do, because electrostatic cohesion binds them together, but once suspended they stay suspended at almost any velocity. This is why a river can scour a sandy bed easily while a clay bank resists, and why floodwater remains muddy long after it has slowed. Sediment transport rises far faster than discharge, typically as discharge raised to a power between about 2 and 3. Doubling the flow may increase sediment transport six to eight-fold. As a result the great majority of a river's annual sediment budget can move in a few days, and a single very large flood can rearrange a channel completely, cutting new courses, abandoning old ones and depositing metres of material on the floodplain. Two consequences matter practically. Deposition on floodplains is what makes them fertile: the annual silt of the Nile sustained Egyptian agriculture for several thousand years until the Aswan High Dam ended it in 1970, after which fertiliser imports had to substitute. And scour is what destroys infrastructure. Bridge failure during floods is dominated not by the force of water on the structure but by scour around the piers and abutments, where locally accelerated flow excavates the bed and undermines the foundation. The collapse of the Schoharie Creek bridge in New York in 1987, which killed ten people, was a pier scour failure, and scour remains the leading cause of bridge loss worldwide. Sediment starvation is the mirror problem. Dams trap the load of the rivers above them almost completely, and the water released below is described as hungry, meaning it has capacity to carry sediment and no sediment to carry, so it takes it from the bed and banks instead. Channels below large dams commonly incise by metres over decades, undermining bridges and lowering the water table beneath the adjacent floodplain. At the coast the same starvation deprives deltas of the material that offsets subsidence and sea-level rise, which is a principal reason the Nile, Mississippi and Mekong deltas are losing land.

sections.heading: Floodplain Ecology and the Flood Pulse
sections.body: Floodplains are among the most biologically productive environments on Earth, and their productivity is caused by flooding rather than merely tolerated despite it. The organising idea is the flood pulse concept, set out by Wolfgang Junk, Peter Bayley and Richard Sparks in 1989, which argues that in large river-floodplain systems the predictable seasonal rise and fall of water is the principal force driving biological production, and that the lateral exchange between channel and floodplain matters more than the downstream transport of material along the channel. The mechanism is straightforward once stated. When water spreads over the floodplain it inundates land that has been drying, decomposing and accumulating nutrients. Those nutrients are released into a warm, shallow, sunlit body of water, which produces an enormous pulse of algal and plant growth, followed by invertebrates, followed by fish. Many river fish species spawn specifically on the rising limb and use inundated vegetation as nursery habitat inaccessible to their predators, then return to the channel as water recedes. In the Amazon, fish including several Colossoma species feed directly on fruits and seeds falling from flooded forest and are significant seed dispersers, an interaction that only exists because the forest floods to depths of ten metres or more for months each year. Riparian vegetation is equally dependent. Cottonwoods and willows of the genera Populus and Salix release seed that remains viable for only days to a few weeks and germinates on freshly deposited moist sediment. Successful recruitment requires a flood that deposits bare sand at the right time of year followed by a recession slow enough that the seedling roots can grow downward faster than the water table falls. Where dams have removed the spring flood peak and stabilised flows, entire cottonwood gallery forests along rivers in western North America have failed to regenerate for decades and are now aging stands with no replacement. Floodplain wetlands also perform functions with direct economic value. They denitrify: anaerobic sediments convert nitrate carried in agricultural runoff into nitrogen gas, and restoring floodplain connectivity is one of the more effective interventions available against downstream eutrophication and coastal dead zones. They store carbon in waterlogged organic soils. They recharge groundwater. And they attenuate floods, which means the ecological and the engineering arguments for keeping floodplains connected point the same direction. This convergence underpins the concept of environmental flows, the deliberate release of water from dams in patterns that mimic natural flood pulses, now practised on rivers including the Colorado, the Murray and the Zambezi with measurable ecological results. There is a direct human dimension to this. Floodplain fisheries feed very large numbers of people, most notably in the Mekong basin, where the annual reversal of the Tonle Sap river in Cambodia inundates a lake that expands severalfold and supports one of the most productive inland fisheries on Earth, supplying a substantial share of the animal protein in the Cambodian diet. Where flood pulses are damped by upstream dams, that productivity falls, and the loss falls hardest on the people with the fewest alternatives.

sections.heading: Structural Defences and the Levee Effect
sections.body: The traditional response to flooding is to build something. The four main structural approaches are embankments, reservoirs, channel modification and diversion, and each buys protection at a cost that is frequently underestimated. Levees, called flood embankments or dykes in different traditions, are earth or concrete walls along the channel that raise its effective capacity. They work well up to their design standard and fail in several distinct ways beyond it. Overtopping is the obvious one, and once water flows over an earth embankment it erodes a breach within minutes. Less obvious and more common is internal failure: seepage through the embankment or underseepage beneath it can carry fine particles out of the structure, forming a growing internal channel in a process called piping that can destroy a levee without any water ever reaching its crest. Slope instability from prolonged saturation and scour at the toe complete the list. Levees also transfer risk. By confining a flood to a narrower cross-section they raise its stage locally and remove floodplain storage, which increases peak discharge downstream, so a levee protecting one town can measurably worsen flooding in the next. And by trapping sediment within the confined channel they can raise the bed over decades until the river runs above the surrounding land, a perched condition seen on the Yellow River, the Po and the lower Mississippi, where failure becomes catastrophic rather than merely damaging. Reservoirs attenuate floods by storing the peak and releasing it slowly, but only if there is empty space when the flood arrives, which conflicts with the desire to keep them full for water supply and power. Operating rules govern this tradeoff, and misjudged releases during an unexpected inflow have caused or worsened floods repeatedly. Channelisation, straightening and deepening a river to move water away faster, reliably speeds the flood downstream and destroys habitat, and has been substantially abandoned as a general strategy. Overarching all of this is the levee effect, sometimes called the safe development paradox, identified by the geographer Gilbert White in his 1945 dissertation Human Adjustment to Floods. Building defences reduces the frequency of small floods, which encourages development on the protected land, which increases the value at risk, so that when a flood exceeding the design standard eventually arrives the damage is greater than it would have been without the defence. White's conclusion, that floods are acts of God but flood losses are largely acts of man, remains the foundational statement of the field. The 1993 Mississippi and Missouri flood is the standard case study. Prolonged rainfall over an already saturated basin produced a flood lasting from roughly April to October, with damages estimated around 15 to 20 billion United States dollars of the time. More than a thousand levees failed or were overtopped, and post-event analysis found that agricultural levees which failed had, in some reaches, inadvertently reduced peak stages by restoring floodplain storage. The event prompted a substantial shift in United States policy toward buyouts and floodplain restoration rather than further embankment.

sections.heading: Non-Structural Measures and Room for the River
sections.body: The alternative to holding water back is to manage exposure to it, and over the past half century this approach has moved from the margins to the mainstream of flood policy. Floodplain mapping is the foundation. In the United States the Federal Emergency Management Agency publishes flood insurance rate maps delineating the Special Flood Hazard Area, the 1 per cent annual chance floodplain, along with the base flood elevation, the water surface height in that event. Within it, a distinction is drawn between the floodway, the channel plus the adjacent land required to convey the flood without raising its level more than a specified amount, typically one foot, and the flood fringe, where development that does not obstruct conveyance may be permitted if elevated. The 0.2 per cent, or five hundred year, zone is also mapped. Comparable systems exist under the European Union Floods Directive of 2007, which requires member states to produce hazard and risk maps and management plans on a six-year cycle. Zoning and building regulation act on those maps. The most effective single measure for existing buildings is elevation of the lowest floor above the base flood elevation plus a margin called freeboard, usually 0.3 to 1 metre, since damage rises very steeply with depth in the first metre. Wet floodproofing accepts water into unoccupied lower levels with flood-resistant materials and openings that equalise pressure; dry floodproofing seals a building, and is only viable to about a metre because hydrostatic pressure on walls becomes structurally unmanageable above that. Buyout and relocation of repeatedly flooded properties is expensive but permanently effective, and studies of United States buyout programmes generally find favourable benefit-cost ratios. The most significant conceptual shift is giving rivers space rather than confining them. The Dutch Room for the River programme, running from about 2007 to 2019 at a cost near 2.3 billion euros across more than thirty locations, deliberately lowered floodplains, relocated dykes landward, dug side channels and removed obstructions in order to reduce flood levels rather than raise defences. Comparable approaches include setback levees, managed realignment, restoring floodplain connectivity, and engineered bypasses such as California's Yolo Bypass, which diverts high flows from the Sacramento River across a wide leveed floodway that is farmland and wildlife habitat the rest of the year, and the Bonnet Carre Spillway above New Orleans, which relieves the Mississippi into Lake Pontchartrain. Insurance and financial instruments belong in this category too, and their design has real effects on behaviour. Where flood insurance is subsidised and priced below actual risk, it removes the financial signal that would discourage building in hazardous places, which is the criticism most consistently made of the United States National Flood Insurance Program. Where it is priced to risk, it becomes unaffordable for exactly the low-income households most exposed. Different countries resolve this differently: the United Kingdom operates a reinsurance pool called Flood Re that caps premiums for eligible homes while explicitly excluding properties built after 2009, so that the subsidy cannot encourage new floodplain development.

sections.heading: Forecasting and Warning: Turning Data into Lead Time
sections.body: A flood forecast is a chain, and it is only as strong as its weakest link. The chain begins with observation, passes through modelling, and ends with a warning that someone acts on. Observation comes from three sources. Rain gauges give accurate point measurements but sample a tiny fraction of the area, and a convective cell can miss every gauge in a catchment. Weather radar gives spatial coverage at kilometre resolution and five to ten minute intervals, but measures reflectivity rather than rainfall and must be converted using empirical relationships that are systematically wrong in hail, in bright-band melting layers and at long range where the beam overshoots low cloud; radar estimates are therefore usually corrected against gauges. Satellites provide global coverage, indispensable in ungauged basins, at coarser resolution and with greater error. River gauges close the loop by measuring what actually happened, and their real-time readings are used to correct model states as a flood develops, a process called data assimilation. Modelling proceeds in two stages. A hydrological model such as HEC-HMS or a distributed physically-based model converts rainfall and antecedent conditions into discharge at points in the network. A hydraulic model such as HEC-RAS then routes that discharge through the channel and floodplain to produce water surface elevations and inundation extents, either in one dimension along a series of cross-sections or, increasingly, in two dimensions across a terrain grid derived from airborne lidar. Two-dimensional modelling on good lidar is a genuine improvement in accuracy, and its main limitation is that terrain data can be a decade old and buildings, walls and culverts are represented imperfectly. Lead time is set by physics, not by effort. In a large basin the water already on the ground determines the flood for days ahead, so forecasts can be skilful several days out and on the largest rivers, weeks. In a small steep catchment the lag time may be under an hour, so any useful warning must be based on forecast rather than observed rainfall, and quantitative precipitation forecasting at that scale remains poor. This is why flash floods kill disproportionately. Modern practice increasingly uses ensembles, running the model many times with perturbed inputs to produce a probability rather than a single number, and flash flood guidance, which computes how much rain in a given period would be required to cause flooding given current soil moisture, then compares that threshold with the forecast. The last link is the one that fails most often. Warnings must reach people who are asleep, who do not speak the official language, who have no phone signal, or who have heard several warnings that came to nothing. Post-event reviews of deadly floods repeatedly find that a technically correct warning was issued and did not translate into action.

sections.heading: How Human Activity Changes Flood Risk
sections.body: Flood risk is a product of hazard, exposure and vulnerability, and human activity alters all three, generally upward. Urbanisation is the clearest and best-quantified effect. Replacing soil and vegetation with roofs and pavement removes infiltration and storage, while drains and culverts deliver water to the channel faster than any natural pathway. The result is a hydrograph with a shorter lag and a much higher peak. Studies of urbanising catchments commonly find peak discharges for frequent events increased by factors of two to five, and stream ecological condition begins to degrade measurably once total impervious cover exceeds roughly 10 per cent of the catchment. Counter-measures grouped as sustainable drainage or low-impact development, including permeable paving, green roofs, swales, detention basins and rain gardens, work by restoring storage and infiltration, and are most effective against the frequent, small events; their influence on extreme events is real but far more modest. Rural land use matters, but the popular version overstates it. Deforestation, soil compaction by machinery and livestock, drainage of wetlands and the straightening of headwater streams all increase runoff and reduce lag. However, the effect is strongest for small and medium events in small catchments and diminishes for extreme events in large basins, because once the soil is saturated it makes little difference what is growing on it. The honest statement is that catchment management can meaningfully reduce frequent flooding and improve water quality and should be pursued, but that it cannot be relied upon to prevent a rare extreme flood in a large basin, and claims that reforestation alone will solve major flooding do not survive examination of the evidence. Climate change acts principally through the atmosphere's water-holding capacity. The Clausius-Clapeyron relation implies that saturation vapour pressure rises about 7 per cent per degree Celsius of warming, and observed increases in extreme short-duration rainfall are broadly consistent with this, sometimes exceeding it for convective events. The translation into flood magnitude is not one-to-one, because floods also depend on snow, soil moisture and seasonality, and observed trends in river flood peaks are genuinely mixed: a major analysis of European data by Bloschl and colleagues published in 2019 found increases in the northwest, decreases in the south and east, and shifts in timing, rather than a uniform signal. Finally, land subsidence lowers the ground relative to the water. Groundwater extraction has sunk parts of Jakarta, Bangkok, Mexico City and California's San Joaquin Valley by metres, and drained organic soils oxidise and shrink. Subsidence converts land that was above flood level into land that is not, silently and permanently. Vulnerability, the third term in the risk equation, is shaped by decisions that have nothing to do with hydrology. Single-storey construction, ground-floor bedrooms, basements used as living space, immobile occupants without transport, buildings with no upper floor to retreat to and communities without warning or evacuation plans all convert the same depth of water into far greater harm. Reducing vulnerability is typically the cheapest available intervention and the least often funded, because it produces no visible structure to point at.

sections.heading: Practical Response: Before, During and After a River Flood
sections.body: Flood danger to people is governed by depth and velocity together, and their product is the standard measure. An adult begins to lose footing once depth in metres times velocity in metres per second exceeds roughly 0.5 to 0.6, children at much less. Thirty centimetres floats many cars and sixty moves most of them, because a floating vehicle has no traction whatever its weight. Floodwater is also contaminated, hides open manholes and scour holes, keeps un-isolated electrics live, and at 15 to 20 degrees Celsius causes disabling hypothermia within hours.
ingredients: Your property's elevation relative to the local base flood elevation, read off the flood map for your area. Whether your floor sits above or below that line changes every other decision.
A grab bag: documents in a waterproof wallet, essential medicines, a torch, a wind-up radio, a power bank, drinking water, warm clothing and sturdy footwear.
A way to receive official warnings that does not need mains power or the internet, plus registration for any national flood warning service.
A meeting point on high ground and an out-of-area contact everyone can call, since local networks congest first.

Knowledge of where to isolate electricity, gas and water, and the tools to do it. Non-return valves on drains and toilets if you own the building, since sewage backflow floods many properties before the river arrives.
steps: Long before any flood, establish whether you are on a floodplain and check whether your insurance covers flood, which in many countries is a separate product standard policies exclude.
On a flood watch, move vehicles to high ground, secure anything that could float away, and lift valuables upstairs. Doing this early is far easier than in the dark in rising water.
On a flood warning, isolate electricity at the consumer unit and gas at the meter before water reaches the sockets, not after. Fill containers with clean water, as supply may be cut or contaminated.
Evacuate when told to, by the route given, and go early. Most flood deaths involve people who left too late or not at all. Take the grab bag and leave everything else.
Never drive into water of unknown depth. If a vehicle stalls in rising water, abandon it at once and move to higher ground; do not try to restart it or retrieve possessions.

If trapped by rising water indoors, go up, but not into a sealed attic without a way onto the roof. Take a torch and something to signal with, and tell emergency services exactly how many people are present.
After the water recedes, do not re-enter until the building is confirmed sound and the electrics checked. Photograph everything before moving it, for the claim.
Wear waterproof gloves and boots to clean up, wash thoroughly afterwards, and discard porous items including mattresses, upholstery and most insulation that contacted floodwater.

Dry the building slowly and completely; masonry holds water for months and mould begins within 24 to 48 hours. Never run a fuel-powered generator, pump or pressure washer indoors or in a doorway, because carbon monoxide poisoning is a recurring and entirely avoidable cause of post-flood death.

sections.heading: Failure Modes, Limits and Common Misconceptions
sections.body: Flood management fails in a small number of recurring ways, and knowing them is more useful than knowing any single technique. The first is trusting the design standard. Every defence has one, and floods larger than it exist. A levee rated for the 1 per cent flood has roughly a 1 per cent annual chance of being overtopped, and a higher chance of failing for some other reason first. Residual risk, the risk that remains behind a defence, is real and is usually the largest single component of total flood risk in a defended area, because that is where the assets are concentrated. The second is treating the flood map boundary as a line between safe and unsafe. The mapped edge of the 1 per cent floodplain is a modelled estimate with substantial uncertainty, often several tens of metres horizontally on flat ground. A house just outside it is not safe; it is slightly less exposed. Analyses of United States flood claims consistently find that a substantial share, frequently cited as around a quarter to a third, come from outside the mapped Special Flood Hazard Area. The third is the belief that a flood has somehow been used up. Return periods are not schedules, and clustering of large floods within a few years is entirely consistent with the statistics and is made more likely by multi-year climatic patterns that leave catchments persistently wet. The fourth is sandbags. They are useful for diverting shallow flowing water and protecting small openings, but they are permeable, laborious, and largely ineffective above about half a metre. A properly sized flood barrier or door guard outperforms a wall of sandbags, and where water is deep enough to load a wall structurally, letting it in deliberately to equalise pressure is often correct: a metre of water outside a solid wall with none inside imposes forces ordinary domestic construction is not designed to resist. The fifth is data. Historical records are short, gauges are sparse in exactly the poor and mountainous regions where floods kill most, rating curves are extrapolated at the extreme end, terrain models are out of date, and stationarity no longer holds. Any specific number for a design flood should be treated as a central estimate within a wide band. The most durable conclusion of a century of flood science remains Gilbert White's: the flood itself is not the disaster. The disaster is the decision to place people and property where the river goes, and then to build a wall and forget why it is there. A sixth failure mode is institutional memory. Defences, warning systems and land-use rules are built after a disaster and then maintained by people who did not experience one. Embankments grow vegetation and animal burrows, culverts silt up, sirens are decommissioned as obsolete, and zoning is relaxed under development pressure, during the long quiet intervals the statistics guarantee. The interval between damaging floods on a given river is frequently longer than a professional career, so knowledge of what the river can do has to be deliberately written down and handed on, because it will not be remembered.

guides.safetyNote: Moving floodwater is far more dangerous than it looks. Roughly 15 centimetres of fast-moving water can knock an adult off their feet and about 60 centimetres will float and sweep away most cars, and a large share of flood deaths occur in vehicles driven into water of unknown depth. Never walk, swim or drive through floodwater, never enter a flooded basement or building where electricity may still be live, and treat all floodwater as contaminated with sewage, fuel and chemicals.
